'''''Potentilla indica''''', known commonly as '''false strawberry''', '''mock strawberry''', or '''Indian strawberry''',{{r|CRC-World2016}} (also '''snakeberry''' in North America{{r|weakley2024}}) is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Rosaceae]],{{r|powo}} native to West Asia to India, East Asia, and Southeast Asia.{{r|CRC-Diversity2025}} It has [[trifoliate|ternate]] foliage and an aggregate [[accessory fruit]], similar to true [[strawberry|strawberries]] of the genus ''[[Fragaria]]''.{{r|fnad}} Unlike the white or slightly pink flowers of true strawberries, ''Potentilla indica'' has yellow [[flower]]s, as do many other [[Potentilla]] species. It is native to eastern and southern [[Asia]], but has [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in many regions worldwide. ''P. indica'' is an invasive species in the United States and Canada,{{r|powo}} often noticed as a weed on grass lawns.

Many sources consider this plant part of the genus ''[[Potentilla]]''{{r|powo}}{{r|weakley2024}} due to evidence from chloroplast genetic sequence data that the genus ''Duchesnea'' is included within ''Potentilla'',{{r|eriksson2003}} though some still list it as '''''Duchesnea indica'''''.{{r|fnad}}{{r|wfo}}{{r|Heo2019}}

==Description==
[[File:Mock Strawberry (Potentilla indica) 08.18.22.jpg|thumb|''Potentilla indica'' bloom]]
The herbaceous plant spreads along creeping [[stolon]]s, rooting and producing plantlets at each node.{{r|fnad}} The leaves are [[trifoliate]], dark green, and somewhat thick.{{r|Heo2019}} The flowers are produced singly on axillary [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]]s. The yellow petals of ''Potentilla indica'' have a nectar guide near the center of each petal that absorbs UV light more strongly than the rest of the petal and is visible only in the UV spectrum.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Naruhashi |first1=Naohiro |last2=Sugimoto |first2=Mamoru |date=1996 |title=The Floral Biology of Duchesnea (Rosaceae)|journal=Plant Species Biology |volume=11 |issue=2–3 |pages=173–184|url=https://esj-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1442-1984.1996.tb00143.x |doi=10.1111/j.1442-1984.1996.tb00143.x |access-date=21 November 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The most common variety, ''Potentilla indica var. indica'', has fruiting receptacles and achenes that are red and glossy.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Barbara Ertter |author2=James L. Reveal |name-list-style=amp |title=Rosaceae In: Flora of North America Editorial Committee, eds. 1993+. Flora of North America North of Mexico [Online] 25+ vols |date=2014 |publisher=Oxford University Press |volume=9 |url=https://floranorthamerica.org/Duchesnea_indica_var._indica |access-date=22 November 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1127/1869-6155/2012/0130-0060 | title=Potentilla L. (Rosaceae) and related genera in Asia (excluding the former USSR), Africa and New Guinea - Notes on Potentilla XXVIII. |last1=Soják | first1=Jiří |journal=Plant Diversity and Evolution | volume=130 | issue=1–2 | pages=7–157 | year=2012}}</ref> The rare variety ''D. indica f. albocaput'' Naruh., with white receptacles and cream achenes, has been reported only in Argentina and Japan.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Debes |first1=Mario A. |last2=Orce |first2=Ingrid G. |last3=Luque |first3=Ana C. |last4=Díaz-Ricci |first4=Juan C. |last5=Castagnaro |first5=Atilio P.|last6=Arias |first6=Marta E. |year=2018 |title=First report of Duchesnea indica f. albocaput (Rosaceae) in Northwestern Argentina |url=https://botanicaargentina.org.ar/first-report-of-duchesnea-indica-f-albocaput-naruh-rosaceae-in-northwestern-of-argentine/ |journal=Boletín de la Sociedad Argentina de Botánica |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=83–91|doi=10.31055/1851.2372.v53.n1.19890 |hdl=11336/101935 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Invasiveness ==
Mock strawberry is considered [[Invasive species|invasive]] in some regions of the [[United States]] and [[Canada]], where it may disrupt local [[Ecosystem|ecosystems]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mock strawberry |url=https://extension.umn.edu/identify-invasive-species/mock-strawberry |access-date=2024-11-23 |website=extension.umn.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=false strawberry, Potentilla indica Rosales: Rosaceae |url=https://www.invasive.org/browse/subinfo.cfm?sub=78283 |access-date=2024-11-23 |website=www.invasive.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Indian Strawberry (Mock Strawberry) |url=https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/indian-strawberry-mock-strawberry |access-date=2024-11-23 |website=Missouri Department of Conservation |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=Potentilla indica |date=2024-08-14 |work=Wikipedia |url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Potentilla_indica&oldid=1240331410#cite_note-11 |access-date=2024-11-23 |language=en}}</ref> Studies have shown that it can negatively impact the abundance of [[Springtail|springtails]] and [[Ant|ants]], affecting soil [[biodiversity]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Landsman |first1=Andrew P. |last2=Schmit |first2=John Paul |last3=Matthews |first3=Elizabeth R |date=2021 |title=Invasive Plants Differentially Impact Forest Invertebrates, Providing Taxon-Specific Benefits by Enhancing Structural Complexity |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution |volume=9 |doi=10.3389/fevo.2021.682140 |doi-access=free}}</ref>[[File:Potentilla_indica_(1).jpg|thumb|Potentilla indica ]]

==Uses==
The fresh berries are edible but considered less palatable than proper strawberries.{{r|fda}}<ref>{{Cite book |author=United States Department of the Army |author-link=United States Department of the Army |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |pages=52 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}}</ref>

The cousin ''[[Potentilla fulgens]]'' is widely distributed in the [[Khasi Hills]] and [[Jaintia Hills]], [[Meghalaya]], northeastern India, where the plants are known in the [[Khasi language|Khasi]] as {{lang|kha|lyniangbru}} (and in English as "Himalayan cinquefoil"{{efn|This common name is perhaps more commonly applied to ''[[Potentilla atrosanguinea]]''.}}), and usage of this species extends to the ''Potentilla'' genus.<ref name="medhi-etal2023"/> Roots of ''Potentilla'' are consumed (chewed) with [[Betel nut chewing|betel nuts]] by the [[Khasi people]], and the ''P. indica'' species is also used in this way.<ref name="CRC-World2016"/>

There is recorded ethno-medicinal usage (in northeastern India) as [[anthelmintic]] to get rid of [[Parasitism|parasites]]<ref name="CRC-World2016"/>{{efn|Other sources list ''[[Potentilla fulgens|P. fulgens]]'' for treatment for intestinal parasites in [[Western Himalayas]], rather than ''P. indica''.<ref name="manikandan-etal2023"/><ref name="medhi-etal2023"/>}} and to treat lung symptoms.<ref name="CRC-World2016"/> A survey conducted in Assam, India, from 2018–2020 documented the use of ''Potentilla indica'' by traditional healers to treat asthma.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Gogoi|first1=Pinki  |last2=Lungphi |first2=Pyonim |last3=Das |first3=A. P. |last4=Ayam |first4=Victor Singh|year=2023 |title=Phytomedicines Used in Respiratory Diseases by Traditional Healers of Lakhimpur and Dhemaji Districts of Assam, India In: Arunachalam, K., Yang, X., Puthanpura Sasidharan, S. (eds) Bioprospecting of Tropical Medicinal Plants|url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-28780-0_7 |publisher=Springer, Cham |pages=227–241 |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-28780-0_7 |isbn=978-3-031-28780-0 | access-date= 22 November 2024 }}</ref> In [[traditional Chinese medicine]], it is used for clearing heat, cooling blood, detumescence, and detoxication.<ref>
